title: Conditional probability as a definition, and the multiplication rule

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Let A and B be events, with P(B) above 0. The conditional probability of A given B, written P(A | B), is the probability of A once you know that B has happened. The vertical bar is read “given”. It is defined as the probability of both, divided by the probability of the condition. The sign ÷ means “divided by”.

P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B)

Knowing B removes every outcome outside B. What is left is a smaller sample space, B itself, and the division rescales it so that it has probability 1 again. Inside B the three rules of section 1 hold again, so P(not A | B) = 1 − P(A | B).

In a two-way table, the probability in one cell, such as P(A and B), is a joint probability: a probability about two events together. A probability about one event alone, read from a row or column total, is a marginal probability. A conditional probability is a joint probability divided by a marginal one.

Multiply both sides of the definition by P(B). This gives the general multiplication rule, which holds for any two events, independent or not.

P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A | B)

The same joint probability can be built in the other order, starting from A.

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A)

A tree diagram draws the multiplication rule in stages. The first split gives the marginal probabilities of one event. Each second split gives the conditional probabilities of the other event, given the first. Multiplying along a path from left to right gives a joint probability.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
“Given B” means: forget everyone who is not B. Among the people left, what share are A? That share is P(A | B).

The order matters.

blocks.alt: Three bars from zero: 36 of 131 is 0.2748, 36 of 59 is 0.6102, 36 of 42 is 0.8571.
blocks.caption: In Kiran’s rebuilt table of 131 men, 36 are both flagged by the arm tape and in the 25-29.9 band. Divided by all 131 men, that is the joint probability 0.2748. Divided by the 59 flagged men, it is P(in the band | flagged), 0.6102. Divided by the 42 men in the band, it is P(flagged | in the band), 0.8571. One top, three bottoms, three different numbers.

blocks.alt: Four bars from zero, one for each path of the tree: in the band and flagged 0.2748, in the band and not flagged 0.0458, not in the band and flagged 0.1756, not in the band and not flagged 0.5038.
blocks.caption: The tree for Kiran’s 131 men, split first by the band (0.3206 in it, 0.6794 not) and then by the tape. Multiplying along each path gives a joint probability: 0.2748, 0.0458, 0.1756 and 0.5038, the four cells of the probability table. The four ends add to 1.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start from the table of Book 0, D3, rebuilt from Kiran and colleagues’ study of 131 men at a medical college in Mangaluru. The tape flags a man whose upper arm measures 31.3 centimetres or more. “In the band” means a body-mass index from 25 to 29.9.

in the band not in the band total
arm 31.3 cm or more 36 23 59
arm under 31.3 cm 6 66 72
total 42 89 131

Pick one of the 131 men at random. Divide every count by 131 to turn the table into probabilities.

36 divided by 131 ≈ 0.2748
23 divided by 131 ≈ 0.1756
6 divided by 131 ≈ 0.0458
66 divided by 131 ≈ 0.5038
42 divided by 131 ≈ 0.3206
59 divided by 131 ≈ 0.4504

in the band not in the band total
arm 31.3 cm or more 0.2748 0.1756 0.4504
arm under 31.3 cm 0.0458 0.5038 0.5496
total 0.3206 0.6794 1

The four inner cells are joint probabilities: P(flagged and in the band) is 0.2748. The row and column totals are marginal probabilities: P(in the band) is 0.3206.

Now ask the clinic’s question. A man is flagged. What is the chance he is in the band? Use the definition: the joint probability divided by the marginal probability of the condition.

0.2748 divided by 0.4504 = 0.6101
36 divided by 59 ≈ 0.6102

About 61 per cent, the positive predictive value of Book 0, D3. The two lines differ in the fourth decimal only because 0.2748 and 0.4504 were rounded. Dividing by 131 and then dividing again cancels the 131, so the formula and the count give the same answer.

Now ask the other question. A man is in the band. What is the chance he is flagged?

0.2748 divided by 0.3206 = 0.8571
36 divided by 42 ≈ 0.8571

About 86 per cent, the sensitivity. P(in the band | flagged) is 0.61. P(flagged | in the band) is 0.86. Same top, 0.2748. Different bottoms, 0.4504 and 0.3206.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The table is rebuilt from the paper’s rounded percentages, not printed by the paper. It holds for these 131 men, students at one college. “Not in the band” includes the 10 men with an index of 30 or more, so “flagged and not in the band” is not the same as “flagged wrongly” for the question “is his index 25 or more?”.

The 61 per cent belongs to this group, in which about 32 per cent of the men are in the band. In a group where fewer men are in the band, the same tape gives a lower figure, as Book 0, D3 showed.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Often you have no table, only a marginal probability and a conditional one. Then the multiplication rule builds the joint probability, and a tree diagram keeps the stages in order.

Split the same 131 men first by the band. On the first split, P(in the band) is 0.3206 and P(not in the band) is 0.6794. On the second split, read each conditional probability from its own column.

36 divided by 42 ≈ 0.8571
6 divided by 42 ≈ 0.1429
23 divided by 89 ≈ 0.2584
66 divided by 89 ≈ 0.7416

Multiply along each of the four paths, left to right.

0.3206 times 0.8571 = 0.2748
0.3206 times 0.1429 = 0.0458
0.6794 times 0.2584 = 0.1756
0.6794 times 0.7416 = 0.5038
0.2748 plus 0.0458 plus 0.1756 plus 0.5038 = 1.0000

The four ends are the four cells of the probability table, and they add to 1. The diagram and the table hold the same information.

Here is the move you will use in clinic, from published figures alone. The paper’s Table 2 prints the share of men in the band as 32.1 per cent. Its abstract prints the sensitivity as 86 per cent. Multiply.

0.321 times 0.86 = 0.2761
0.2761 times 131 = 36.2

About 36 men are both in the band and flagged, as the rebuilt table says. The small gap comes from the two rounded percentages.

You could equally split the men first by the tape: P(flagged) is 0.4504, then P(in the band | flagged) is 0.6102.

0.4504 times 0.6102 = 0.2748

The same joint probability, built in the other order. That is the fact Bayes’ theorem will turn into a formula, three sections on, in section 5.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Multiplying a prevalence by a sensitivity gives the joint probability only for the group both numbers describe. Here both describe the same 131 men. A prevalence from one place and a sensitivity from a study elsewhere give a joint probability that is only as good as the assumption that the test behaves the same in both places.

points.html: “P(A | B) and P(B | A) are the same number, said two ways” is the error. They share a top and divide it by different bottoms. Before you quote a conditional, say aloud what it is conditioned on.
The denominator of a conditional is the condition. Dividing a cell by the grand total gives a joint probability, a different and usually smaller number.

You can build the chance of “both” from a marginal and a conditional: P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A | B). Use it when a paper gives a prevalence and a sensitivity but no table. Then rebuild the table as counts and check that the counts are whole people.
The multiplication rule needs no independence. What independence changes is only that P(A | B) may be replaced by P(A).
Before you quote a conditional for your clinic, ask whose table it came from.
When you read “x per cent of those who…”, the group after “of those who” is the condition. Rewrite the sentence as P(… | those who …) before you repeat it.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “86 per cent of the men in the band were flagged, so a flagged man has an 86 per cent chance of being in the band.” The first is P(flagged | in the band). The second asks for P(in the band | flagged). They share the top, 36 men, and divide it by different bottoms: 42 men in the band, 59 men flagged. In Kiran’s men the second is about 61 per cent.

blocks.label: Reporting it
blocks.html: Kiran and colleagues measured 131 men. An arm circumference of 31.3 cm or more flagged 36 of the 42 men with a body-mass index from 25 to 29.9 (86 per cent). Of the 59 men it flagged, 36 were in that band (61 per cent). The second figure comes from a table rebuilt from the paper’s percentages.

blocks.prompt: From memory: write the definition of P(A | B) and the general multiplication rule. Then say in one sentence why P(A | B) and P(B | A) are usually different numbers.
blocks.answer:
P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B), for P(B) above 0.

P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A | B), and equally P(A) × P(B | A).

The two conditionals share the top, P(A and B), and divide it by different bottoms, P(B) and P(A). They are equal only when P(A) equals P(B), or when A and B never happen together, so that both are 0.

blocks.prompt:
A district report on a made-up screening camp says: “Of the 400 adults screened, 120 had a raised blood sugar. Of these, 90 had overweight. In all, 160 adults had overweight.”

Write each number as a probability for an adult picked at random from the 400: say which are marginal, which joint and which conditional. Then work out the chance that an adult with overweight had a raised blood sugar, and say why it is not 90 divided by 120.
blocks.answer:
120 divided by 400 = 0.3
160 divided by 400 = 0.4
90 divided by 400 = 0.225
90 divided by 120 = 0.75

P(raised sugar) is 0.3 and P(overweight) is 0.4: marginal. P(raised sugar and overweight) is 0.225: joint. P(overweight | raised sugar) is 0.75: conditional, on the 120 with a raised sugar.

The question asks for the other conditional: the condition is now “overweight”.

0.225 divided by 0.4 = 0.5625
90 divided by 160 = 0.5625

About 56 per cent. 90 divided by 120 answers “of those with a raised sugar, how many were overweight”. The question asked “of those overweight, how many had a raised sugar”, so the bottom is 160.

What the report does not show: anything about adults who were not screened, or why the two go together.

blocks.prompt: In a group of 100 people, 20 are both A and B, 30 are A but not B, 10 are B but not A, and 40 are neither. Work out P(A | B) and P(B | A).
blocks.answer:
The people who are B: 20 plus 10. The people who are A: 20 plus 30.

20 plus 10 = 30
20 plus 30 = 50
20 divided by 30 ≈ 0.6667
20 divided by 50 = 0.4

P(A | B) is 0.6667 and P(B | A) is 0.4. The top, 20, is the same.

blocks.prompt: P(A and B) is 0.12 and P(B) is 0.4. Work out P(A | B).
P(B) is 0.25 and P(A | B) is 0.6. Work out P(A and B).
blocks.answer:
Use the multiplication rule, P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A | B).

0.25 times 0.6 = 0.15

P(A and B) is 0.15.

blocks.prompt: P(A and B) is 0.18 and P(A | B) is 0.45. Work out P(B).
blocks.answer:
The multiplication rule says 0.18 = P(B) × 0.45. Divide both sides by 0.45.

0.18 divided by 0.45 = 0.4

P(B) is 0.4. Check it: 0.4 times 0.45 is 0.18.

blocks.prompt: P(B) is 0.3. P(A | B) is 0.5 and P(A | not B) is 0.2. Draw a tree diagram that splits first by B, and work out the four joint probabilities at its ends. Check that they add to 1.
blocks.answer:
On the first split, P(B) is 0.3 and P(not B) is 1 minus 0.3. On each second split, the two conditionals add to 1.

1 minus 0.3 = 0.7
1 minus 0.5 = 0.5
1 minus 0.2 = 0.8
0.3 times 0.5 = 0.15
0.3 times 0.5 = 0.15
0.7 times 0.2 = 0.14
0.7 times 0.8 = 0.56
0.15 plus 0.15 plus 0.14 plus 0.56 = 1

P(B and A) is 0.15, P(B and not A) is 0.15, P(not B and A) is 0.14 and P(not B and not A) is 0.56. They add to 1.

blocks.prompt: In Kiran’s rebuilt table of 131 men, 36 are flagged by the arm tape and in the 25-29.9 band, and 42 are in the band. Work out P(flagged and in the band) and P(in the band) as probabilities for a man picked at random. Then use the definition to work out P(flagged | in the band), and say what it is called.
blocks.answer:
36 divided by 131 ≈ 0.2748
42 divided by 131 ≈ 0.3206
0.2748 divided by 0.3206 = 0.8571

P(flagged | in the band) is about 0.857, or 86 per cent of the men in the band. It is the sensitivity, as the paper prints it.

blocks.prompt:
For women, Kiran’s Table 2 gives 151 women, 41 of them with a body-mass index from 25 to 29.9. The paper’s cut-off for women is an arm circumference of 28.5 cm, with sensitivity 88 per cent and specificity 83 per cent. As for the men, these fit the 41 women in the band against the other women.

Rebuild the four cells of the table as whole numbers of women. Then work out the chance that a woman the tape flags is in the band.
blocks.answer:
The women not in the band:

151 minus 41 = 110

The women in the band whom the tape flags: 88 per cent of 41, to the nearest woman, checked by dividing back.

0.88 times 41 = 36.08
36 divided by 41 ≈ 0.878

36 rounds back to 88 per cent. The women outside the band whom the tape clears: 83 per cent of 110.

0.83 times 110 = 91.3
91 divided by 110 ≈ 0.827

91 rounds back to 83 per cent. The rest follow by subtraction.

41 minus 36 = 5
110 minus 91 = 19
36 plus 19 = 55

in the band not in the band total
arm 28.5 cm or more 36 19 55
arm under 28.5 cm 5 91 96
total 41 110 151

The chance that a flagged woman is in the band divides by the flagged row.

36 divided by 55 ≈ 0.6545

About 65 per cent of the women the tape flags are in the band. The table is rebuilt from rounded percentages, as the men’s was.

blocks.prompt: Kiran’s Table 2 prints the share of men in the 25-29.9 band as 32.1 per cent. The abstract prints the arm tape’s specificity as 74 per cent. Use the multiplication rule to work out the probability that a man picked at random is outside the band and wrongly flagged. Then turn it into a number of the 131 men, and compare it with the rebuilt table’s 23.
blocks.answer:
Outside the band: 1 minus 0.321. Wrongly flagged, given outside the band: 1 minus the specificity.

1 minus 0.321 = 0.679
1 minus 0.74 = 0.26
0.679 times 0.26 = 0.1765
0.1765 times 131 = 23.1

The probability is about 0.177, which is about 23 men of the 131, as the rebuilt table has. The 0.1 of a man comes from the rounded percentages.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

Kiran’s rebuilt table: 36 men flagged and in the band, 42 in the band, 59 flagged
question: a man is flagged; what is the chance he is in the band?
P(in the band | flagged) = 36 divided by 42 = 0.857
so about 86 per cent of flagged men are in the band
blocks.answer:
The third line broke. The condition is “flagged”, so the bottom is the 59 flagged men, not the 42 in the band.

36 divided by 59 ≈ 0.6102

About 61 per cent. The working computed P(flagged | in the band), the sensitivity.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: 86 per cent is the number the paper prints, and the top line, 36, is right for both questions. Only the bottom changes, and the working took the bottom from the wrong total.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

131 men: P(in the band) = 0.3206, so P(not in the band) = 0.6794
sensitivity 0.86, specificity 0.74
P(flagged and not in the band) = 0.6794 times 0.86 = 0.5843
so about 77 of the 131 men are flagged though outside the band
blocks.answer:
The third line broke. It multiplies the chance of being outside the band by the sensitivity, which is P(flagged | in the band). The second split needs the conditional for men outside the band: P(flagged | not in the band), which is 1 minus the specificity.

1 minus 0.74 = 0.26
0.6794 times 0.26 = 0.1766
0.1766 times 131 = 23.1

About 23 men, as in the rebuilt table, not 77. A check would have caught it: 77 men flagged outside the band is more than the 59 the tape flags in all.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: “flagged” appears in both, so the sensitivity looks like the chance of being flagged. On a tree diagram, each second split needs the conditional for its own first-stage group.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a camp screens 500 adults; 100 have a raised sugar, and 60 of those have overweight
P(overweight | raised sugar) = 60 divided by 500 = 0.12
so 12 per cent of adults with a raised sugar have overweight
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. Dividing by the 500 screened gives P(overweight and raised sugar), a joint probability. The condition is “raised sugar”, so the bottom is the 100 with a raised sugar.

60 divided by 100 = 0.6

60 per cent of adults with a raised sugar have overweight. The figures are made up.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: dividing by the number screened is the habit of every prevalence. It gives a true number, 12 per cent of all adults are both. It answers a different question.

blocks.prompt:
A news item reports Kiran and colleagues’ study: “The arm-tape test was 86 per cent accurate: 86 per cent of the young men it flagged had overweight.”

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what the corrected number does not establish.
blocks.answer:
The paper’s 86 per cent is the sensitivity, P(flagged | in the 25-29.9 band). The news item states P(in the band | flagged). Compute that from the rebuilt table.

36 divided by 59 ≈ 0.6102

About 61 per cent of the men the tape flagged were in the band, not 86 per cent. “Accurate” names neither conditional, so the sentence should name the one it means.

What the 61 per cent does not establish. It comes from a table rebuilt from rounded percentages, for 131 men at one college. “In the band” means 25 to 29.9. It leaves out the 10 men at 30 or more. So for the question “is his index 25 or more?”, 61 per cent is the least the share could be. And it holds only where about a third of the men are in the band; where fewer are, it is lower.

blocks.prompt:
A speaker at a meeting says: “Two in three of our patients with diabetes have overweight. So a patient with overweight has a two-in-three chance of having diabetes.”

Suppose, in a made-up clinic, 10 per cent of patients have diabetes and 30 per cent are overweight. Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
The first sentence gives P(overweight | diabetes), 0.667. The second claims P(diabetes | overweight). Build the joint probability with the multiplication rule, then divide by the other condition.

2 divided by 3 ≈ 0.6667
0.1 times 0.6667 = 0.06667
0.06667 divided by 0.3 = 0.2222

In this clinic a patient with overweight has about a 22 per cent chance of diabetes, not 67 per cent. The two conditionals share the top, 0.0667, and divide it by 0.1 and by 0.3.

What this does not establish. The 10 and 30 per cent are made up; with the clinic’s own figures the answer changes, and the speaker gave none. Neither conditional says whether being overweight raises the chance of diabetes. That needs a comparison with patients who are not overweight, and even then an association is not a cause.
